This room is unoccupied tonight, he thought, or, whoever the person sleeping in it may be, that person is awake now. Thus there is no longer any need to take precautions on that person's account; he must only try not to be heard by the people sleeping in the other rooms.

He went down, placed his ladder against one of the shutters, climbed back up and, passing his hand through the heart-shaped opening, had the good fortune to find fairly quickly the wire attached to the hook that held the shutter closed. He pulled this wire; it was with inexpressible joy that he felt that the shutter was no longer fastened and was yielding to his effort. I must open it little by little, and make my voice recognizable. He opened the shutter wide enough to put his head through, repeating in a low voice: It is a friend.

By listening carefully, he made certain that nothing disturbed the profound silence of the room. But decidedly there was no night-light, even a half-extinguished one, in the fireplace; it was a very bad sign.

Beware the gunshot! He reflected for a moment; then, with his finger, he dared to tap on the pane: no answer; he tapped harder. Even if I must break the pane, this must be brought to an end. As he was tapping very hard, he thought he glimpsed, amid the extreme darkness, something like a white shadow crossing the room. At last there was no longer any doubt: he saw a shadow that seemed to be advancing with extreme slowness. Suddenly he saw a cheek pressed against the pane on which his eye rested.

He started, and drew back a little. But the night was so black that, even at that distance, he could not make out whether it was Madame de Rênal. He feared an initial cry of alarm; for some moments he had heard the dogs prowling and growling softly around the foot of his ladder.

“It is I,” he repeated loudly enough, “a friend.”

No answer; the white phantom had disappeared.

“Deign to open the window for me; I must speak to you; I am too unhappy!” And he struck the pane hard enough to break it.

A slight, dry sound was heard; the window fastening gave way; he pushed open the casement and leapt lightly into the room.

The white phantom was moving away; he seized its arms; it was a woman. All his notions of courage vanished. If it is she, what will she say? What became of him when he understood from a little cry that it was Madame de Rênal?

He clasped her in his arms; she was trembling, and scarcely had the strength to push him away.

“Wretched man! What are you doing?”

Her convulsive voice could barely articulate these words. Julien saw in it the truest indignation.

“I have come to see you after fourteen months of cruel separation.”

“Go, leave me this instant. Ah! Monsieur Chélan, why did you prevent me from writing to him? I would have forestalled this horror.” She pushed him away with truly extraordinary strength. “I repent of my crime; Heaven has deigned to enlighten me,” she repeated in a broken voice. “Go! Flee!”

“After fourteen months of misery, I shall certainly not leave you without having spoken to you. I want to know everything you have done. Ah! I loved you enough to deserve this confidence... I want to know everything.”

Despite Madame de Rênal, this tone of authority held sway over her heart.

Julien, who was holding her tightly with passion and resisting her efforts to free herself, ceased clasping her in his arms. This movement reassured Madame de Rênal a little.

“I am going to take away the ladder,” he said, “so that it does not compromise us if some servant, awakened by the noise, makes the rounds.”

“Ah! Go, go instead,” she said to him with genuine anger. “What do men matter to me? It is God who sees the dreadful scene you are subjecting me to, and who will punish me for it. You are cowardly taking advantage of the feelings I once had for you, but which I no longer have. Do you hear me, Monsieur Julien?”

He was taking away the ladder very slowly so as not to make any noise.

“Is thy husband in town?” he said to her, not in order to defy her but carried away by old habit.

“Do not speak to me in that way, I beg you, or I shall call my husband. I am already only too guilty for not having driven you away, whatever might have come of it. I pity you,” she said to him, seeking to wound his pride, which she knew to be so irritable.

This rejection of his addressing her with thou, this abrupt way of breaking a bond so tender and on which he still relied, drove Julien’s transport of love to the point of delirium.

“What! Is it possible that you no longer love me?” he said to her with one of those accents of the heart that are so difficult to hear unmoved.

She did not answer; as for him, he wept bitterly.

Truly, he no longer had the strength to speak.

“Thus I am completely forgotten by the only being who has ever loved me! What is the use of living henceforth?” All his courage had left him as soon as he no longer had to fear the danger of encountering a man; everything had vanished from his heart except love.

He wept for a long time in silence; she heard the sound of his sobs. He took her hand; she tried to withdraw it; and yet, after a few almost convulsive movements, she left it in his. The darkness was extreme; they were both seated on Madame de Rênal’s bed.

What a difference from what it was fourteen months ago! Julien thought; and his tears redoubled. Thus absence surely destroys every human feeling! It is better for me to go away.

“Deign to tell me what happened to you,” Julien finally said in a voice almost extinguished by grief.

“Certainly,” Madame de Rênal replied in a harsh voice, whose tone held something dry and reproachful for Julien, “my transgressions were known in the town when you left. There had been so much imprudence in your actions! Some time afterward, when I was in despair, the venerable Monsieur Chélan came to see me. For a long time he tried in vain to obtain a confession. One day, he had the idea of taking me to that church in Dijon where I made my First Communion. There, he dared to speak first...”

Madame de Rênal was interrupted by her tears.

“What a moment of shame! I confessed everything. That good man deigned not to crush me beneath the weight of his indignation: he grieved with me. At that time, I wrote you letters every day which I did not dare send you; I hid them carefully, and when I was too unhappy, I shut myself in my room and reread my letters.”}泉析室内开奖直播法国 stendhal 小说段落。完整翻译成准确英语。重点 love 分类。只 JSON。Need ensure
